content: The field of view, also referred to as the field of vision, represents the angular extent of the observable environment that can be seen at any given moment. The field of view varies among different species, depending on the anatomical placement of their eyes. Humans possess a nearly 180-degree forward-facing field of view, whereas certain bird species have a complete or nearly complete 360-degree field of view. Additionally, the vertical range of the field of view can differ between species. The visual capabilities within a field of view are not uniform and vary significantly across species. For instance, in humans, binocular vision, which is crucial for depth perception, encompasses only 140 degrees of the field of view. The remaining 40 degrees of peripheral vision lack binocular overlap, as the images from each eye do not converge in these areas. In contrast, birds with a 360-degree field of view may have only 10 to 20 degrees of binocular vision. Similarly, the ability to perceive color, shape, and motion is not evenly distributed across the field of view. In humans, color vision is concentrated in the central visual field, while motion detection is more pronounced in the peripheral regions. This is due to the higher density of color-sensitive cone cells in the fovea, the central region of the retina, compared to the higher density of motion-sensitive rod cells in the peripheral retina. Since cone cells require significantly brighter light to function, peripheral vision becomes relatively stronger than binocular vision in low-light conditions, such as at night. Optical instruments, such as binoculars and spotting scopes, often specify their field of view in two ways: angular field of view and linear field of view. The angular field of view is typically expressed in degrees, while the linear field of view is a ratio of lengths. For example, an 8-degree angular field of view might be described as having a linear field of view of 305 feet per 1,000 yards or 102 millimeters per meter. For fields of view less than approximately 10 degrees, conversion formulas can be used to switch between angular and linear measurements. In astronomy, the field of view is generally expressed as an angular area observed by an instrument, measured in square degrees or, for higher magnification instruments, in square arc-minutes. For example, the Wide Field Channel on the Advanced Camera for Surveys aboard the Hubble Space Telescope has a field of view of 10 to 15 square arc-minutes. Ground-based survey telescopes, however, often have much wider fields of view. The photographic plates used by the UK Schmidt Telescope had a field of view of 30 square degrees. The 8-meter Pan-STARRS telescope, equipped with one of the most advanced digital cameras, has a field of view of 7 square degrees. Until recently, digital cameras could only cover a smaller field of view compared to photographic plates, although they surpass photographic plates in quantum efficiency, linearity, dynamic range, and ease of processing.
